entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14960"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.5.1-John.5.47">Joh 5:1-47</reference>. The Impotent Man Healed--Discourse Occasioned by the Persecution Arising Thereupon.</title> <div sID="gen28850" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14960"/><hi type="bold">1. a feast of the Jews--</hi>What feast? No question has more divided the Harmonists of the Gospels, and the duration of our Lord's ministry may be said to hinge on it. For if, as the majority have thought (until of late years) it was a Passover, His ministry lasted three and a half years; if not, probably a year less. Those who are dissatisfied with the Passover-view all differ among themselves what other feast it was, and some of the most acute think there are no grounds for deciding. In our judgment the evidence is in favor of its being a Passover, but the reasons cannot be stated here. <div eID="gen28850" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14963"/><div sID="gen28855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14963"/><hi type="bold">4. an angel, &c.--</hi>This miracle differed in two points from all other miracles recorded in Scripture: (1) It was not one, but a succession of miracles periodically wrought: (2) As it was only wrought "when the waters were troubled," so only upon one patient at a time, and that the patient "who first stepped in after the troubling of the waters." But this only the more undeniably fixed its miraculous character. We have heard of many waters having a medicinal virtue; but what water was ever known to cure instantaneously a single disease? And who ever heard of any water curing all, even the most diverse diseases--"blind, halt, withered"--alike? Above all, who ever heard of such a thing being done "only at a certain season," and most singularly of all, doing it only to the first person who stepped in after the moving of the waters? Any of these peculiarities--much more all taken together--must have proclaimed the supernatural character of the cures wrought. (If the text here be genuine, there can be no doubt of the miracle, as there were multitudes living when this Gospel was published who, from their own knowledge of Jerusalem, could have exposed the falsehood of the Evangelist, if no such cure had been known there. The want of <reference osisRef="John.5.4">Joh 5:4</reference> <hi type="bold">and part of <reference osisRef="John.5.3">Joh 5:3</reference> in some good manuscripts, and the use of some unusual words in the passage, are more easily accounted for than the evidence in their favor if they were not originally in the text. Indeed <reference osisRef="John.5.7">Joh 5:7</reference> is unintelligible without <reference osisRef="John.5.4">Joh 5:4</reference>. The internal evidence brought against it is merely the unlikelihood of such a miracle--</hi>a principle which will carry us a great deal farther if we allow it to weigh against positive evidence). <div eID="gen28855" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 4. an angel, &c.-- This miracle differed in two points from all other miracles recorded in Scripture: (1) It was not one, but a succession of miracles periodically wrought: (2) As it was only wrought "when the waters were troubled," so only upon one patient at a time, and that the patient "who first stepped in after the troubling of the waters." But this only the more undeniably fixed its miraculous character. We have heard of many waters having a medicinal virtue; but what water was ever known to cure instantaneously a single disease? And who ever heard of any water curing all, even the most diverse diseases--"blind, halt, withered"--alike? Above all, who ever heard of such a thing being done "only at a certain season," and most singularly of all, doing it only to the first person who stepped in after the moving of the waters? Any of these peculiarities--much more all taken together--must have proclaimed the supernatural character of the cures wrought. (If the text here be genuine, there can be no doubt of the miracle, as there were multitudes living when this Gospel was published who, from their own knowledge of Jerusalem, could have exposed the falsehood of the Evangelist, if no such cure had been known there. The want of Joh 5:4 and part of Joh 5:3 in some good manuscripts, and the use of some unusual words in the passage, are more easily accounted for than the evidence in their favor if they were not originally in the text. Indeed Joh 5:7 is unintelligible without Joh 5:4 . The internal evidence brought against it is merely the unlikelihood of such a miracle-- a principle which will carry us a great deal farther if we allow it to weigh against positive evidence).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14969"/><div sID="gen28863" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14969"/><hi type="bold">10-16. The Jews--</hi>that is, those in authority. (See on <reference osisRef="John.1.19">Joh 1:19</reference>.)<div eID="gen28863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it is not lawful to carry thy bed--</hi>a glorious testimony to the cure, as instantaneous and complete, from the lips of the most prejudiced! (And what a contrast does it, as all our Lord's miracles, present to the bungling miracles of the Church of Rome!) In ordinary circumstances, the rulers had the law on their side (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.15">Ne 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.21">Jr 17:21</reference>). But when the man referred them to "Him that had made him whole" (<reference osisRef="John.5.11">Joh 5:11</reference>) as his authority, the argument was resistless. Yet they ingeniously parried the thrust, asking him, not who had "made him whole"--that would have condemned themselves and defeated their purpose--but who had bidden him "take up his bed and walk," in other words, who had dared to order a breach of the sabbath? It is time we were looking after Him--thus hoping to shake the man's faith in his Healer. <div eID="gen28864" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14995"/><div sID="gen28916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14995"/><hi type="bold">39-42. Search the scriptures, &c.--</hi>"In the Scriptures ye find your charter of eternal life; go search them then, and you will find that I <hi type="bold">am the Great Burden of their testimony; yet ye will not come to Me for that life eternal which you profess to find there, and of which they tell you I am the appointed Dispenser." (Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.17.11">Ac 17:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.12">12</reference>). How touching and gracious are these last words! Observe here (1) The honor which Christ gives to the Scriptures, as a record which all have a right and are bound to search--</hi>the reverse of which the Church of Rome teaches; (2) The opposite extreme is, resting in the mere Book without the living Christ, to direct the soul to whom is its main use and chiefest glory. <div eID="gen28916" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 39-42.
